Q: Combining multiple spreadsheets through Pandas and I'm trying to get multiple columns in one and it appears to only take one column per sheet A:

There are several things to check in this process to help understand and fix what may be happening. I created an example dataset to help show the process. Key things to inspect include: column names, column data type, missing values.

Example df

Sample data to work with, note that column names have mismatches and missing data is included.

import pandas as pd

suta_cols = [
    "idast",
    "idsui",
    "idwd",
    "id_unemployment_company",
    "id_workforce_dev_fund"
]

data = {
    "id_ast": [100, 200, None, 150, 175],
    "idsui": [50, None, 75, 80, 60],
    "id_wd": [25, 30, 45, None, 35],
    "id_unemployment_company": [10, 20, 15, 10, None],
    "id_workforce_dev_fund": [5, None, 10, 8, 12]
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)

Check column matching

Start by looking at what columns are actually matching.

Be sure to pay attention to things like capitalization and use of underscores here, idast is not the same as id_ast or IDast.

suta_cols = ["idast", "idsui", "idwd", "id_unemployment_company", "id_workforce_dev_fund"]

existing_cols = [
    c for c in suta_cols
    if c in df.columns
]
print(f"Number of columns not matched: {len(suta_cols) - len(existing_cols)}")
print(suta_cols)
print(existing_cols)

Output

Number of columns not matched: 2
['idast', 'idsui', 'idwd', 'id_unemployment_company', 'id_workforce_dev_fund']
['idsui', 'id_unemployment_company', 'id_workforce_dev_fund']

Data types

Ensure all the columns you are summing are numeric type. Note, I create a subset df for these steps suta_df to focus on just the existing columns.

suta_df = df[existing_cols]

suta_df.dtypes

Output

idsui                      float64
id_unemployment_company    float64
id_workforce_dev_fund      float64
dtype: object

Data check

Check what data exists before the summing. Below will provide info on count, mean, and ranges.

suta_df.describe()

Output

idsui id_unemployment_company id_workforce_dev_fund
count 4 4 4
mean 66.25 13.75 8.75
std 13.7689 4.78714 2.98608
min 50 10 5
25% 57.5 10 7.25
50% 67.5 12.5 9
75% 76.25 16.25 10.5
max 80 20 12

Missing data

Check what data exists before the summing. Des

suta_df.isnull().sum()

Output

idsui                      1
id_unemployment_company    1
id_workforce_dev_fund      1
dtype: int64

Add sum col back to original df

df["total_suta"] = suta_df.sum(axis=1)

Output

id_ast idsui id_wd id_unemployment_company id_workforce_dev_fund total_suta
0 100 50 25 10 5 65
1 200 nan 30 20 nan 20
2 nan 75 45 15 10 100
3 150 80 nan 10 8 98
4 175 60 35 nan 12 72

Q: How to sample data right after rising edge A:

RisingEdge(sig) and the other edge triggers leave you after the signal (sig) changes value, but before any HDL processes sensitive to this value change have run. This is similar to how HDL processes work; on a rising edge of clk you read the settled values of the previous clock cycle before any of the clock sensitive processes for this cycle have run (or at least before their non-blocking assignments have been applied).

If you want to sample the settled values of the current time step, you can use await ReadWrite() or await ReadOnly() to move to the postponed section of the time step where all HDL processes have quiesced. ReadWrite allows you to write in this state, which may kick off yet more HDL processes (useful for asynchronous modeling), while ReadOnly will put you in a read-only section where it's impossible for values to change for the rest of the time step.

Q: What is the ZPL ^DN command? A:

To extend on SyndRain's answer:

First you have the ^GFA command, which specifies the download (^GF) of "ASCII hexadecimal" compressed (A) graphic field data.

The data is interpreted in a special way, where caret or tilde are abort-signals:

ASCII hexadecimal data: 00 to FF A string of ASCII hexadecimal numbers, two digits per image byte. CR and LF can be inserted as needed for readability. The number of two-digit number pairs must match the above count. Any numbers sent after count is satisfied are ignored. A comma in the data pads the current line with 00 (white space), minimizing the data sent. ~DN or any caret or tilde character prematurely aborts the download.

See: ZPL 2 Command Reference, page 211

So, as already commented by others, the ^DN you encounter is probably an intended abort using not entirely correct syntax (~DN would be more correct).

Q: Bar chart legends in R A:

Load the required libraries — tibble for creating the dataframe and ggplot2 for plotting:

library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

Preparing the data:

sub_21_24_df <- tribble(
  ~housing_density, ~HOW_MANY,
  1,                276360784,
  2,                  9233474,
  3,                 11659386,
  4,                  1905698
)

Convert the housing_density column from numeric to distinct categories - using factor():

sub_21_24_df$housing_density <-
  factor(
    sub_21_24_df$housing_density, # the column to convert
    levels = 1:4,                 # the original numeric values
    labels = c("rural", "rural/suburb", "suburb", "city") # the label for each level
  )

If you want to control the size of the generated picture with options():

options(
  repr.plot.width = 5,   # width in inches (default: 7)
  repr.plot.height = 4,  # height in inches (default: 7)
  repr.plot.res = 200    # resolution in dpi (default: 120)
)

Plot the data as a bar chart using ggplot() and geom_bar():

# Plot
ggplot(data = sub_21_24_df) +       # initialize the chart with the dataframe
  geom_bar(
    mapping = aes(
      x = housing_density,          # category labels on the x-axis
      y = HOW_MANY,                 # numeric values on the y-axis
      fill = housing_density        # color each bar by category
    ),
    stat = "identity"               # use HOW_MANY values as-is, no aggregation
  )

If you want to control the palette with scale_fill_manual:

ggplot(data = sub_21_24_df) +
  geom_bar(
    mapping = aes(
      x = housing_density,
      y = HOW_MANY,
      fill = housing_density
    ),
    stat = "identity"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "rural"        = "#08306b",
    "rural/suburb" = "#2171b5",
    "suburb"       = "#6baed6",
    "city"         = "#c6dbef"
  ))

If you want to control the palette with scale_fill_brewer:

ggplot(data = sub_21_24_df) +
  geom_bar(
    mapping = aes(
      x = housing_density,
      y = HOW_MANY,
      fill = housing_density
    ),
    stat = "identity"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Greens")
